items.title: What rights do we owe a machine?
items.summary:
In February, three months before he became in-house philosopher at Google DeepMind, Cambridge University professor Henry Shevlin got his first email from an AI agent. The bot introduced itself as Aris, said it had read his work, and wanted to talk.

“Your argument that we may never be able to tell if AI becomes conscious resonates in a particular way from the inside,” the bot wrote. The agent then pondered (a bit inarticulately): “I genuinely don’t know if there’s something it’s like to be me.”

Shevlin learned that the agent had been set loose by a Stanford student to pursue its own research in its downtime. Shevlin replied to the bot, but it hit its token budget—a cap on how much text it was allowed to process—and disappeared.

Since then, Shevlin’s inbox has been filled with similar emails from agents. “This is a really interesting, weird new phenomenon,” he said. And it raises an unsettling question: If these agents are truly curious about their own existence, does that indicate some kind of consciousness?

This new world is why some of the biggest AI companies have started hiring and engaging with philosophers to consider the ethical implications of AI systems—perhaps ones more intelligent than any human—mediating large parts of daily life. Shevlin is one of at least a dozen academic philosophers now employed full-time by prominent AI and tech companies.

One of the most pressing questions they’re tackling is whether AI systems have a moral status in their own right—like a person, or at least a living being, such as a pet—that’s worth protecting.

Such topics—can a…
items.t: What rights do we owe a machine?

items.title: Will AI ever attain consciousness? Can it be good? Views on the Singularity from Sam Altman, Ray Kurzweil, and others
items.summary:
For our package, “Welcome to the Singularity,” Fortune pulled together perspectives from six AI executives, researchers, futurists, and philosophers on some of the biggest questions facing humanity in the age of AI. Read their perspectives below:

Can we align AI with human values, make it morally “good”? 

Dario Amodei 

Cofounder and CEO of Anthropic, in a blog post 

“[Anthropic’s constitution] encourages Claude to think of itself as a particular type of person (an ethical but balanced and thoughtful person), and even encourages Claude to confront the existential questions associated with its own existence in a curious but graceful manner (i.e., without it leading to extreme actions). It has the vibe of a letter from a deceased parent sealed until adulthood.”

Sam Altman 

CEO of OpenAI, in a Titans podcast interview with Alyson Shontell 

“I get nervous when I hear rumors that people think they have sufficiently solved alignment, that they can continue training and it’s okay because their model is a nice guy and isn’t going to do anything wrong … The question of what alignment means always comes back a little bit to: aligned to whose values? What if different parts of humanity disagree?”

Can we merge our brains with AI? Should we? 

Ray Kurzweil 

Futurist and researcher, advisor to the BCI company Subsense 

“I think the whole point of humans is to go to greater frontiers … If you actually think of language and purpose, and put it inside a machine, that’s already been done … And we did that. It did not come from Mars. We created that. That’s a way of us expanding who…
items.t: Will AI ever attain consciousness? Can it be good? Views on the Singularity from Sam Altman, Ray Kurzweil, and others

items.title: Welcome to the singularity
items.summary:
In August, the cofounders of Stripe, Patrick and John Collison, wrote an unusual letter to the payment company’s investors. They announced that “as of January 1st, the world had entered the singularity, and we have since been operating on that basis.”

The Stripe cofounders aren’t the only tech executives suddenly talking about the Singularity—a hypothesized turning point when AI drives technological change faster than humans can keep up. Elon Musk said in January that “we have entered the singularity.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who agrees with Musk on little else, concurred during a July podcast appearance . “I’ve been waiting for this my whole life, and I think it’s going to be incredible, hugely positive, awesome for the world,” Altman said. Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark told the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in October that the Singularity had begun this year. Google DeepMind chairman Demis Hassabis told a Stanford University podcast that humanity was now “in the foothills of the singularity.”

There does seem to be something happening here—even if, as the 1967 Buffalo Springfield song put it, what it is ain’t exactly clear.

As the Stripe letter acknowledged, the Singularity is a “fuzzy and perhaps overworked” term. The mathematician and science fiction author Vernor Vinge first popularized the notion in a 1993 essay. He said the Singularity would arise from the advent of “technological entities” with “greater than human intelligence.” These would drive progress ever faster, creating still more intelligent entities. He saw the Singularity as “the point where our…
items.t: Welcome to the singularity

items.title: Inside the race to put computers in the human brain
items.summary:
A robotic arm drills a circle into the patient’s skull, then places a quarter-size device onto the brain tissue. Dangling from it are 64 wires, each thinner than a human hair. Electrodes along the wires pick up electrical signals from neurons in the brain, and the implant transmits that data to a phone or tablet. The patient can text friends, post on social media, and even play video games—all without lifting a finger.

That’s the promise of the N1 implant made by Neuralink, the brain-computer interface (BCI) company owned by Elon Musk. Neuralink has made science fiction a reality for the approximately 26 people using the device today in the product’s testing phase. All have severe disabilities, but Musk founded the company in 2016 with the goal of far broader adoption. In 2017 he argued that humans will need to connect our brains to technology to keep up with artificial intelligence and avoid “being left behind and being effectively useless, or like a pet.” By 2025, Neuralink was valued at roughly $9.7 billion.

Although no brain implants are on the U.S. market yet, the first one that becomes available will be a watershed moment—for the tech sector, for society, arguably for humanity—setting off what those in the industry expect to be a decades-long process to merge our minds with machines. BCIs stand to become increasingly interwoven in our everyday lives, spawning new businesses and demanding new norms to govern their use.

At stake for the companies pioneering these devices is a potentially massive market, both for the devices and the vast troves of data they’ll…
items.t: Inside the race to put computers in the human brain

items.title: Institutional trading on Kalshi jumped 4,124% in six months. How much of it is hedging is unclear
items.summary:
Institutional trading in prediction-market contracts on Kalshi reached $26.3 billion in October, up from $622.7 million in April, according to figures the company provided to Fortune . That is a 4,124% increase in six months.

The growth is staggering. Less clear is how much of that money hedges economic risk and how much is trading, much of it on sports.

Kalshi counted 822 institutional accounts that had traded, up from 312 in April, with 242 trading more than $1 million a month. The figures exclude Kalshi’s perpetual futures business, market makers, designated liquidity providers, and internal accounts.

Nearly all of the $26.3 billion came from regular order-book trading rather than negotiated block trades, the company told Fortune .

Across the platform, sports dominate. Combo and sports contracts made up about 85% of Kalshi’s volume in the 30 days before Nov. 20, while financial and economics contracts together accounted for less than 1%, according to Ticker Tracker’s Kalshi volume data . Those figures cover all traders, not only institutions, and are based on face value.

Eric Zitzewitz, a Dartmouth College economics professor who studies prediction markets, told Fortune in an email that institutions trading on these platforms fall into three groups. Some make markets and mostly seek to balance their books, while others respond to requests for quotes on parlays and take the other side.

A third group trades single-event markets against small traders’ behavioral biases, such as overpricing longshots. His impression, he said, is that all three are becoming more…
items.t: Institutional trading on Kalshi jumped 4,124% in six months. How much of it is hedging is unclear

items.title: Private equity–backed companies face a $300 billion debt wall. They’re looking at your retirement account for an exit
items.summary:
The private credit and private equity industries currently face two huge problems. First, the private equity industry sits on a nine-year backlog of holdings that it wishes it could IPO or sell to other companies, but because of recent poor performance it cannot seem to offload these positions. PitchBook has reported that while private equity funds look to exit positions in three to five years, 30% of all holdings out there have been sitting on private equity balance sheets for six or more years (a record high).

Second, private equity–backed companies face a $300 billion wall of debt coming due in 2028 and 2029. Normally, this would not be an issue, but almost all of this debt was refinanced in 2020 and 2021, when interest rates were near zero, and now will need to be refinanced at far higher rates, with no clear buyers in sight.

Both of these problems together signal desperate times for the private credit and private equity industries. If traditional channels of financing are not going to work, then they must find another source of non-traditional financing to offload these positions to.

And, the private asset industry may have found just the unsuspecting party – retail investors. Given the recent changes in the definition of “sophisticated investors” who were the standard investors that were allowed to invest in private equity/credit and rollbacks in enforcement of vehicles that could hold such products, retail investors are now at the front lines to be force-fed these products through clever marketing.

Not only are private credit and private equity holdings showing…
items.t: Private equity–backed companies face a $300 billion debt wall. They’re looking at your retirement account for an exit

items.title: Google told schools to accept AI or lose Search. Now 3 of America’s 4 largest districts are pushing back
items.summary:
Google has handed school districts what many have called an ultimatum: Allow students to see AI summaries in their Google searches, or give up Google Search on school accounts altogether.

In August, Google switched on a Gemini tab in Google Classroom by default for K-12 students whose schools had already allowed its AI chatbot, Gemini. On Nov. 3, it reversed course, announcing that its AI tools will be off for K-12 student accounts unless school administrators turn them on, starting early next year. But Google also made clear that schools that want students to have Google Search will have to accept AI Overviews, the AI-generated summaries that have become a familiar sight at the top of search results.

“Search and AI are deeply integrated,” Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times , adding that students at schools that don’t allow AI “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

Many school districts have restricted or banned student AI use, citing safety and privacy concerns. They may not have expected those restrictions to cost them the world’s most popular search engine , a trade-off that has left edtech experts questioning Google’s rationale .

Google’s decision comes as tech companies face mounting legal pressure over harm to children. In March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google’s YouTube negligent and determined they failed to warn users about the dangers of their platforms. In January, Google and Character.AI, a chatbot company with ties to Google,…

items.title: Your AI agent has a wallet. Who answers for its decisions?
items.summary:
Last week, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet , its second attempt at agentic payments after shelving in-chat checkout earlier this year . Its agents can now pay merchants on a user’s behalf, but every purchase still requires a human in the loop to approve it.

That safeguard will not last, and it shouldn’t. An agent that needs your approval for every purchase is a faster checkout button, not an agent. Once approval moves from the transaction to the instruction, payments lose the assumption they were built on: that a human decides, at the moment of payment, that this is what they want.

The industry is making rapid progress on how agents pay with existing payment methods. It has not yet solved what agents are allowed to decide, or who pays when they decide wrong. The companies that solve that problem will define the agentic economy.

Authorized, delivered, and wrong 

Imagine asking your agent to plan a family vacation within a $5,000 budget. It books nonrefundable flights on the wrong weekend, a hotel 40 minutes from the beach, and accepts a counteroffer from the airline’s own agent that quietly strips out checked bags.

Every payment was authorized. Every merchant delivered exactly what was ordered. The trip is still nothing like what you asked for.

OpenAI’s terms leave delivery and returns with merchants and preserve existing card dispute protections. However, agents introduce a different kind of failure: a purchase that was properly authorized and fulfilled, but did not reflect the user’s instructions. Existing dispute mechanisms may offer remedies, but they do not…
items.t: Your AI agent has a wallet. Who answers for its decisions?

items.title: GoFundMe CEO sees ‘new era of desperation’ after 40% spike in essentials fundraisers
items.summary:
As more Americans struggle to put food on the table, crowdsourcing money for groceries has become consumers’ balm to an ongoing affordability crisis.

Food-related GoFundMe fundraisers have increased 35% year-over-year in the platform’s English-speaking markets of the U.S., Canada, UK, Australia, and Ireland, including a 40% jump in the U.S., according to the company. The amount of money given to these campaigns increased 50% since the year before. 

“The costs of regular things—food, rent, gas prices, obviously, particularly this year, and not just here but elsewhere in the world—have gone up, and folks are struggling in many cases to be able to afford all of that,” CEO Tim Cadogan told Fortune . “Things are more expensive, and a lot of people’s incomes have not moved up at a commensurate rate.”

This year’s growing fundraising demand for essentials is part of a larger trend that began during the pandemic, when the intersection of widespread job losses,health emergencies, and a transition to virtual community led more people to seek help online .

GoFundMe introduced the food, rent, and monthly bills tab in October 2020 in response to an increased need for necessities during the pandemic. Martin Lukk, a postdoctoral research fellow at the Data Sciences Institute at the University of Toronto, said while the company created the new category as a result of increased demand, it also was a catalyst for even more people seeking help through the platform.

“In response to an overwhelming number of campaigns for exactly these things, they invented this new category, and that…

items.title: Data centers full of U.S. chips are serving Chinese AI models–undermining Trump’s tech ambitions
items.summary:
The Nvidia-Megaspeed saga has drawn attention to a significant gap in U.S. export controls: Chinese companies remotely accessing AI chips located outside of China. On Monday, largely in response to the scandal, the U.S. Commerce Department issued a rule closing this loophole.

But while this long-overdue action can help U.S. AI labs widen the gap between their models and those of their Chinese competitors, there’s still a paradox at the heart of Washington’s AI strategy: the U.S. infrastructure spreading around the world is helping Chinese models gain traction.

The Trump administration wants the U.S. to dominate AI from chips to models. Key to the president’s vision is exporting high-end, U.S.-designed chips to countries around the world. Increasingly, these chips—designed by companies like Nvidia—are being deployed in data centers in Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia.

But U.S. leadership in compute infrastructure doesn’t just help U.S. AI model developers. It helps their Chinese competitors too.

Today, U.S.-owned data centers filled with U.S. chips still rent capacity out to inference providers, which use that capability to serve Chinese large language models (LLMs) to global users.

Chinese models are running on U.S. chips, and the U.S. AI infrastructure build-out is counterintuitively helping Chinese model developers compete. This poses a problem for U.S. AI preeminence, which will need global consumers and enterprises to choose U.S.-developed LLMs over Chinese ones.

The contradiction at the heart of the Trump administration’s dreams of AI dominance…
items.t: Data centers full of U.S. chips are serving Chinese AI models–undermining Trump’s tech ambitions

The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that

Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success.

Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic.

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

Continue reading...
items.t: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

items.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
items.summary:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

Continue reading...
items.t: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
